The Erouti Model

A rules-based way to trade NQ in the New York morning, using levels that come from the previous day high, confirmed by market structure and order flow.

Learn the basics first.This is a strategy guide, not a beginner course. Before you use it you should already understand: candlesticks, support and resistance, how futures contracts and tick values work, order types (market, limit, stop), how to place a stop, and what a drawdown is. If any of that is new, spend a few weeks on free basics first, then come back. Without them this will not make sense and you will lose money.

What this guide is, and is not

  • It is my method: Auction Market Theory (AMT), volume profile (VP) extremes, previous-day levels with digit levels, and footprint as the final confirmation.
  • It does not teach pattern recognition. That comes from hours on a live chart, watching where price reacts and where it probably wants to go. I tell you what to look for. Your eyes have to be trained on the chart. Plan on at least a month of daily screen time before trading it live.
  • Its goal is mainly to avoid losses, not to make wins bigger. By taking only well-positioned levels at the extremes of a balance, you skip the low-quality trades in the middle of the range, which is where most accounts bleed.
Honest status.This method is a hypothesis you test yourself. Nothing here guarantees profit, a payout or a pass. Trading futures carries a high risk of loss and you can lose more than you put in.

The method in six lines

1
Mark PDH and PDL before the open. PDH matters most.
2
Take the last two digits of the PDH and draw that ending every 100 points near price. These are your digit levels.
3
Use them for the NY AM session only, roughly 9:30 to 11:00 ET.
4
Check AMT and VP. Keep only levels at the extreme edges of a balance. Skip anything in the middle.
5
Wait for the footprint to confirm the pattern at the level (absorption, stacked imbalances, failure to continue).
6
One trade, stop at structure, size from the stop. Then you are done.

The method, in detail

Diagrams and extra detailEvery concept here has a full diagram and a longer explanation in the DEEP DIVE tabs in the sidebar (AMT, volume profile shapes, setups with a to-scale trade chart, footprint patterns, order flow, the Oct 30 example).

1. The levels: PDH first, PDL second

The previous day high (PDH) is the most important reference in this method. It is the price where the last full session ran out of buyers, so traders remember it, place orders around it and defend it. The previous day low (PDL) is the mirror image and is used as a secondary reference, mainly as a target or a second area of interest.

Digit levels, step by stepPDH = 29,794.25. Keep the last two digits of the whole number: 94. Mark every 100 points near price: 28,694 / 28,794 / 28,894. Tomorrow the PDH changes, so the digits change too. Never reuse yesterday's digits. Use the calculator in the Daily tools tab.
Be honest with yourself.NQ moves hundreds of points a day, so price crosses a level every 100 points all the time. A digit level on its own proves nothing. That is exactly why the next two filters exist, and why you should test the digits against random endings (for example 17, 52, 68) on your own data. If random endings work just as well, the edge is in the filters, not the digits.
🔒 VAULT NOTE · Why the PDH is specialThink about who is watching it. Breakout traders put entries above it, shorts put stops above it, and breakdown sellers wait below it. When price reaches it, several groups act in the same few points. Your job is not to guess which group wins. It is to wait until the footprint shows who did.

2. Time window: NY AM only

Trade the digit levels from the 9:30 ET open until about 11:00 ET. This is when volume is highest, spreads are tight and levels get tested hardest. After 11:00 volume fades and the levels lose weight. Outside the window you do nothing. Not trading is part of the system.

3. Filter one: Auction Market Theory

A market is an auction. Price moves to find where buyers and sellers agree to trade lots of volume. It spends most of its time in balance (a range where value is accepted) and sometimes leaves in imbalance (a trend) until a new balance forms.

IdeaWhat it means for you
Balance and value areaThe range holding about 70% of volume. The edges are where the opportunities are. The middle is chop.
Open locationOpen inside yesterday's value: expect rotation, fade the edges. Open outside it: either it is accepted and trends, or it fails and returns to value.
AcceptancePrice trades outside an area and builds time and volume there. The old edge becomes support or resistance.
Rejection / excessA fast move away from a price, leaving a tail. The market said no. Stops often get swept first, then price reverses.
Initiative vs responsiveInitiative traders push price out of balance. Responsive traders fade it. Know which one is in control before you take the level.

4. Filter two: volume profile extremes

Draw the weekly profile first (it is the map), then the daily (the zoom). Mark POC, VAH, VAL and the high and low volume nodes. Then grade every digit level:

GradeWhere the digit level sitsAction
AAt an extreme edge of a weekly balance (VAH, VAL, weekly high or low)Full plan, normal size
BNot weekly, but at a daily balance edgeReduced size
CIn the middle of a balance, or in a low volume node where price travels fastSkip. No exceptions.

The point of this filter: a level in the middle of a range has no one defending it and no trapped traders to fuel a reaction. It is where good traders get chopped up. Skipping those trades does not make your wins bigger, it removes losses.

Use one session definition (regular hours or full session) and never switch, or your edges move and stop being comparable day to day. Also note: if price leaves the weekly range there is no weekly volume to read, so decide your rule in advance (for example use the daily profile only and half size).

5. Confirmation: footprint patterns

The levels and the profile tell you where. The footprint tells you whether the other side is actually there. It shows bid and ask volume at each price inside each candle, and needs tick data. Use the same settings every day (bid x ask, delta, imbalance highlighting around 300%).

PatternWhat you seeMeaning
AbsorptionVery heavy aggressive volume at one price, price refuses to travelA large passive player is soaking it up. Confirm the next candle fails to trade through.
Stacked imbalances3 or more consecutive prices where one side dominatesReal control. The start of the stack often becomes a defended price on return.
Unfinished auctionZero volume on one side at a candle's extremeMarket often returns to finish it. Do not fade it immediately.
Delta divergenceNew price extreme, delta does not agreeWarning only. Never an entry on its own.
ExhaustionVolume dries up as price pushes to a new extremeThe attackers have run out.
You have to learn this on the chart.I cannot teach pattern recognition in text. Do this: week 1, only read footprints and name what you see on 10 candles a day. Week 2, mark every digit level and screenshot each reaction with the footprint. Week 3, replay or simulator, only A-grade levels. Week 4, count which confirmations worked and which failed, then decide. Review at least 20 examples of each pattern before you trust it.

Common mistakes: seeing absorption everywhere (volume is high at every level on a busy day), trading without the level, judging a pattern from one candle, and changing settings after a loss.

6. The three setups

SetupEntryStop
ReversalPrice touches the level, a candle closes back on the side it came from, footprint shows absorptionBeyond the level plus a buffer
Sweep and reclaimPrice breaks the level, takes stops, closes back through with delta flippingBeyond the sweep extreme (known at entry)
Break and retestCandle closes beyond the level, quiet pullback to it with no opposite stackBack through the level

7. Management

  • Stop at a structure point, never a random number. A flat 20 point stop on NQ is a guess.
  • Size from the stop, never the other way round (see Daily tools).
  • Target the next level, POC or balance edge, at least 1.5R away. If it is less, skip it.
  • Take half at 1R, then move the stop to breakeven only after a candle closes past 1R.
  • A candle closing through the stop zone cancels the idea even before the stop is touched.
  • One trade a day. When it is done, win or lose, you are done.

8. When you do not trade

  • No A or B level near price. A no-trade day is a good day.
  • Red-folder news before noon, until the reaction is clear.
  • Price is in the middle of the range.
  • Footprint does not confirm. Log it as "no confirmation".
  • You are past 11:00 ET, or already took your trade, or you hit your daily limit.

Proof before you trust it

  1. Fix numbers for "reaction", stop and target before testing.
  2. Test 300 or more days, with commission and slippage.
  3. Run the placebo: same rules on random endings.
  4. Build on about 70% of days and test the other 30% untouched.
  5. Report win rate, average win and loss, profit factor, drawdown, losing streaks and trade count.

The prop-firm plan

Prop firms let you trade their capital after you pass an evaluation. Used with discipline and small risk, they are a cheap way to trade size you could not fund yourself. This is the one-trade-a-day way to use them.

Read this first.Evaluations are simulated accounts. Most people who buy them do not get paid, and rules differ by firm and change often. Check your firm's profit target, trailing drawdown, daily loss limit, consistency rule, minimum days and payout rules yourself before you start. Nothing here promises a pass or a payout.

The idea

Instead of grinding for weeks, you look for one high-quality trade per day, and only on an A-grade level. You pass the evaluation with a small number of well-chosen days, then keep the same routine once funded. The edge is selectivity and size control, not speed.

The rules

RuleSetting
Trades per day1 maximum. Win or lose, you are done.
Quality filterA-grade digit level, VP and AMT edge, footprint confirmed (all required boxes)
Risk per tradeAt most 50% of your daily loss limit (DLL), taken from the stop distance
TargetAt least 1.5R, ideally 2R. Take half at 1R.
Day endStop at +1R or at -0.5R if it hits, whichever comes first
After a big winnerClose the platform. No second trade.

Daily flow

The math that decides everything

Your DLLRisk per trade (50%)Target at 2RMNQ at 30 pt stop
$300$150$3002 contracts ($120 risk)
$500$250$5004 contracts ($240 risk)
$1,000$500$1,0008 contracts ($480 risk)
Why never risk more than the DLL.If you risk $2,000 on a trade with a $300 DLL, one loss breaches the account. "No stop" means the loss is whatever the market gives you: on NQ, 100 points is $2,000 per contract, and fast days move much further. A DLL is enforced after the damage, it is not a stop. A 1:2 plan needs a win rate above 33% to break even, before costs, and one trade a day gives you few samples, so results swing.
Figure C. Risk per trade versus the daily loss limit (example: $300 DLL)
🔒 VAULT NOTE · The consistency trapMany traders pass an evaluation with one huge day, then find that consistency rules delay or cut the payout. A sequence of ordinary 1R to 2R days is worth more than one lucky day. Read the rule first, then plan so that no single day is much more than a third of total profit.

Phase 1: the evaluation

  • Size to the firm's rules, not your hopes. Fast passes come from a few A-grade days, not from oversizing.
  • Know the trailing drawdown and where it resets. It is usually what ends accounts.
  • Check the minimum trading days. Some firms do not let you finish in two days.
  • Do not take B grades just to speed up. Slow is allowed.

Phase 2: funded

  • Same routine, same size. Do not increase size because the capital feels like free money.
  • Check the consistency rule. Many firms cap how much one day can be of your total profit, so one huge day can delay a payout.
  • Withdraw on the firm's schedule and treat payouts as results, not as a target.
  • Keep a buffer above the drawdown before raising risk, if at all.

Mistakes that kill accounts

  • Sizing off the target, not the stop.
  • Two trades "to make it back" after a loss.
  • Trading outside NY AM because the day felt slow.
  • Opening many accounts and over-risking them all at once on the same idea.
  • Ignoring a rule you did not read.

Track it as its own log

Trades, R result, days near the drawdown or DLL, evaluations bought, evaluations passed, payouts actually received, total fees paid. Evaluate the whole cost, not only the wins. Show the losing days too.

30-day training plan

This guide cannot teach pattern recognition in text. This plan gives you the reps. Do not trade live money until you finish it.

Week 1 · Learn to see (no trading)

DayTask
1Set up your platform: footprint, volume profile (weekly and daily), PDH, PDL and digit levels. Same settings every day from now on.
2Label today's open type (inside value, outside value) and whether the market is in balance or imbalance. Write one sentence why.
3Draw the weekly profile. Mark POC, VAH, VAL and every high and low volume node. Grade three levels A, B or C.
4Footprint day 1: find 10 examples of absorption on past candles. Screenshot each one with what happened next.
5Footprint day 2: find 10 examples of stacked imbalances and 10 of unfinished auctions. Note which ones were followed by a reaction and which were ignored.
6Review the week. Which patterns were obvious, which were confusing? Re-read the matching tab.
7Rest. No charts.

Week 2 · Mark and record (still no trading)

  • Before 9:30 ET every day: write the gameplan with the PDH digits and the grade of every level near price.
  • During NY AM: only observe. For every digit level price touches, screenshot the footprint and note: reaction (yes or no), size of the reaction in points, and whether a checklist-valid trade existed.
  • After: write one paragraph. What did the market do, and what would I have done?

Week 3 · Simulator with rules

  • Trade only in simulator or replay. One trade a day, A or B levels only, full checklist.
  • Size from the stop with the size calculator. Never the other way round.
  • Score the process after every day: right level, right grade, footprint confirmed, stop respected, size respected, one trade only. Track the score out of six.

Week 4 · Review and decide

  • Count: days traded, trades taken, process score average, R result, trades skipped correctly, rule breaks.
  • List your three most common mistakes and one rule that fixes each.
  • Decide: keep practicing, go live at the smallest size, or adjust the plan.
Ready for live money? All must be true.
20 sessions in a row with a process score of 5 out of 6 or better · no rule breaks in the last 10 sessions · a written plan with your daily loss limit · risk per trade at most half of that limit · you can name your three most common mistakes without looking.
Tip.After week 4 keep the loop going: plan before the open, observe, review after. Traders improve by repeating a small routine, not by adding indicators.

Glossary

Words used in this guide, in plain language.

Absorption
Heavy aggressive volume at a price that fails to move it. A large passive player is taking the other side.
Acceptance
Price trades outside an area and builds time and volume there. The market agrees on the new value.
AMT
Auction Market Theory. Price moves to find the area where buyers and sellers agree to trade.
Balance
A range where the market accepts value and rotates between its edges.
Delta
Volume traded at the ask minus volume traded at the bid, for a candle or a price.
DLL
Daily loss limit. The most a prop-firm account may lose in one day.
Drawdown
The fall from a peak. Trailing drawdown follows your highest balance and is what ends most accounts.
Footprint
A chart showing bid and ask volume at each price inside each candle.
HVN / LVN
High and low volume nodes. HVNs slow price, LVNs let it move fast.
Imbalance
One side trades much more than the other at neighboring prices, often shown at about 300%.
Initiative / responsive
Initiative traders push price out of balance. Responsive traders fade it.
MNQ / NQ
Micro and full-size Nasdaq 100 E-mini futures. MNQ is $2 per point and NQ is $20 per point.
NY AM
New York morning session, roughly 9:30 to 11:00 ET in this guide.
PDH / PDL
Previous day high and low.
POC
Point of control. The price with the most volume in a profile.
R
Your initial risk on a trade. A 2R trade makes twice what it risked.
Rejection
A fast move away from a price that leaves a tail. The market said no.
Sweep
Price pushes through a level to take stops, then returns.
Unfinished auction
A candle extreme with volume on one side only. Price often returns to finish it.
VAH / VAL
Value area high and low. The edges of the area holding about 70% of volume.
Value area
The price range holding about 70% of a profile's volume.

FAQ

Can a complete beginner use this?Not yet. Learn candlesticks, futures contracts, order types and risk first. Then use the 30-day plan before you trade.
How much money do I need?The guide works with micro contracts (MNQ), so size scales down. What you can afford to lose is your limit, and you should never trade money you need.
Why only NY AM?That is when volume and participation are highest and levels get tested hardest. Fewer hours also means fewer chances to overtrade.
Why the previous day high?It is the clearest point where the last full session ran out of buyers, and many traders watch it. That attention is what you are testing.
Are the last two digits magic?No. They give you a fixed, repeatable grid of levels every 100 points. The filters (AMT, volume profile, footprint) decide which of those levels you take. Test the digits against random endings to see how much the grid itself adds.
What if no level is at an extreme?Then you do not trade. A no-trade day is a valid result.
What if price is outside the weekly range?There is no weekly volume to read. Use the daily profile only and trade half size, or skip the day. Decide the rule in advance.
Can I use it on ES or other markets?It was designed for NQ. Test any other market separately before trusting it.
How many trades should I take?One a day at most. When it is done, you are done.
Does it guarantee a payout or a pass?No. Nothing in this guide does. Trading futures carries a high risk of loss.

CHAPTER 01Introduction to Auction Market Theory

1.1 What is Auction Market Theory?

Auction Market Theory (AMT) is a framework for understanding how financial markets operate.

The central idea is simple:

Markets move to facilitate trade and discover fair value.

Every transaction requires a buyer and a seller. However, their willingness to transact changes constantly.

When buyers become more aggressive, they may accept increasingly higher prices.

When sellers become more aggressive, they may accept increasingly lower prices.

The market continuously searches for a price where sufficient buyers and sellers are willing to participate.

That process is called the auction.

1.2 The two main objectives of the market

The market has two fundamental objectives:

1. Facilitate trade

The market attempts to bring buyers and sellers together so transactions can occur.

2. Discover value

The market explores different prices until it finds an area where sufficient participation develops.

These two objectives explain why markets alternate between ranging and trending conditions.

1.3 Important principle

AMT is not a standalone entry strategy.

It is a framework for understanding market behavior.

A trader should use it to determine:

  • Where the market has previously accepted price.

  • Where price has been rejected.

  • Whether the market is balanced or imbalanced.

  • Whether new value is developing.

  • Whether buyers or sellers are showing initiative.

  • Where the current auction may be searching for liquidity and participation.

CHAPTER 02The Mechanics of the Auction

2.1 Buyers and sellers

There are two primary sides of every market transaction.

Aggressive buyers: Buyers willing to pay the available asking price.

Aggressive sellers: Sellers willing to accept the available bid price.

Aggressive activity can move price when available liquidity is insufficient to absorb it.

However, aggressive buying alone does not guarantee that price will rise. Passive sellers may absorb buying pressure.

Likewise, aggressive selling does not guarantee that price will fall.

The response of the opposing side matters.

2.2 How price moves

Consider this simplified sequence:

  1. Buyers become more aggressive.

  2. Offers are consumed.

  3. Price moves higher.

  4. New sellers appear.

  5. If sellers absorb buying and price stops advancing, the auction may begin to balance.

The opposite can happen during aggressive selling.

2.3 The three important variables

Variable Meaning
Price Advertises trading opportunities
Time Shows how long the market accepts prices
Volume Shows how much business is conducted

These three variables form the foundation of Market Profile analysis.

CHAPTER 03Fair Value and Price Discovery

3.1 What is fair value?

Fair value is the area where the market facilitates substantial trading activity.

It is not necessarily the fundamental value of an asset.

It is an observed area of market acceptance.

When price spends considerable time and volume accumulates around a region, that region becomes important.

The market generally spends more time facilitating trade around accepted prices than at temporary extremes.

3.3 Price discovery

Price discovery happens when the market moves outside previously accepted value to explore new prices.

Two possible outcomes exist:

  • Acceptance: the market establishes business at the new prices.

  • Rejection: the market fails to establish business and moves away.

This distinction is extremely important.

A breakout is not confirmed simply because price moves above resistance or below support.

You need to observe what happens after the breakout.

CHAPTER 04Balance vs. Imbalance

4.1 Balanced auction

A balanced market exists when buyers and sellers are relatively comfortable transacting within a particular price region.

Characteristics:

  • Sideways price movement.

  • Repeated rotations.

  • Developing volume around a central area.

  • Overlapping distributions.

  • Limited directional progress.

Illustration:

text

HIGH
|
┌───────────┐
│ ↗ ↘ │
│ ↗ ↙ │
│ ↖ ↗ │
│ ↙ ↖ │
└───────────┘
|
LOW

BALANCE

In balance, traders generally study the extremes and the middle of the range.

The middle is often where two-sided activity is greatest.

4.2 Imbalanced auction

An imbalanced market develops when one side becomes more aggressive and price moves directionally.

Characteristics:

  • Directional price movement.

  • Less overlapping price action.

  • Range expansion.

  • Developing value migrating.

  • Potential single-print areas.

4.3 The difference

Balance Imbalance
Two-sided trade Directional activity
Rotational movement Directional movement
Value relatively stable Value migrating
Range development Range extension
Acceptance around existing prices Search for new prices

Neither condition is automatically bullish or bearish.

The location and direction of the auction determine the context.

CHAPTER 05The Auction Cycle

Markets continuously alternate between balance and imbalance.

text

BALANCE

↓
INITIATIVE ACTIVITY
|
↓
IMBALANCE
|
↓
PRICE DISCOVERY
|
↓
NEW ACCEPTANCE
|
↓
NEW BALANCE
|
↓
NEXT IMBALANCE

5.1 Stage one: Balance

The market establishes an accepted price region.

5.2 Stage two: Imbalance begins

New information or aggressive participation causes price to leave the established range.

5.3 Stage three: Price discovery

The market explores higher or lower prices.

5.4 Stage four: Acceptance

The new prices attract enough participation to facilitate trade.

5.5 Stage five: New balance

A new distribution forms.

The process repeats.

Important: A market can remain imbalanced for a long time. Never assume that a trend must immediately return to balance.

CHAPTER 06Volume Profile

6.1 What is Volume Profile?

Volume Profile displays the amount of volume traded at each price level over a selected period.

Unlike a traditional volume histogram, which displays volume over time, Volume Profile displays volume horizontally by price.

It helps identify:

  • Areas of high participation.

  • Areas of low participation.

  • Price acceptance.

  • Price rejection.

  • Potential areas of rotation.

6.2 Point of Control (POC)

The POC is the price level with the highest traded volume in the selected profile.

It represents the most actively traded price.

Illustration:

text

PRICE VOLUME

105 ██
104 ███
103 █████
102 █████████
101 █████████████
100 ███████████████ ← POC
99 ██████████
98 █████
97 ██

The POC can serve as a reference for potential rotation and acceptance.

It is not guaranteed to attract price.

6.3 Value Area (VA)

The Value Area is conventionally defined as the region containing approximately 70% of the selected profile's volume.

Its boundaries are:

  • VAH: Value Area High.

  • VAL: Value Area Low.

text

VAH

│ │
│ VALUE │
│ AREA │
│ │

VAL

POC inside

The exact calculation can vary by platform and methodology.

6.4 High Volume Node (HVN)

An HVN is an area containing relatively high traded volume.

It often represents price acceptance.

Potential characteristics:

  • Slower price movement.

  • Rotational activity.

  • Repeated trading.

  • Areas where price may consolidate.

6.5 Low Volume Node (LVN)

An LVN is an area containing relatively low traded volume.

It often represents limited acceptance.

Potential characteristics:

  • Faster price movement through the region.

  • Separation between high-volume distributions.

  • Potential rejection or rapid traversal when revisited.

6.6 Naked POC

A naked POC is a previous profile's POC that has not subsequently been revisited.

It is a historical reference level.

It can become a potential objective, but there is no guarantee that price will return to it.

CHAPTER 07Market Profile and TPO

7.1 What is TPO?

TPO stands for Time Price Opportunity.

Market Profile organizes market activity according to the prices visited during specific time brackets.

A common convention is a 30-minute bracket.

Each bracket is represented by a letter.

For example:

  • A = first 30 minutes.

  • B = second 30 minutes.

  • C = third 30 minutes.

  • D = fourth 30 minutes.

Each letter is placed at the prices traded during that bracket.

7.2 Example of a TPO distribution

text

PRICE TPO

105 D
104 CD
103 BCD
102 ABCD
101 ABCDE
100 ABCDE
99 ABCD
98 BCD
97 CD
96 D

The longest row represents the TPO Point of Control.

The distribution helps visualize where the market spent time.

7.3 TPO vs. Volume Profile

TPO Volume Profile
Measures time at price Measures volume at price
Uses time brackets Uses traded volume
Shows duration of acceptance Shows participation
Builds Market Profile Builds Volume Profile

Both are useful because time and volume provide different information.

CHAPTER 08Important Market Profile Levels

8.1 VAH

Value Area High.

The upper boundary of the value area.

Questions to ask:

  • Does price hold above VAH?

  • Does it return into value?

  • Does volume increase above VAH?

  • Is the market accepting higher prices?

8.2 VAL

Value Area Low.

The lower boundary of the value area.

Questions to ask:

  • Does price hold below VAL?

  • Does it quickly return into value?

  • Are sellers maintaining control?

  • Is new value developing lower?

8.3 POC

Point of Control.

The price with the highest TPO count or volume, depending on the profile being used.

Always distinguish TPO POC from Volume POC.

8.4 Initial Balance (IB)

The Initial Balance is commonly the range established during the first hour of a chosen regular trading session.

It is often represented by the first two 30-minute TPO brackets.

text

IB HIGH
┌────────────┐
│ │
│ INITIAL │
│ BALANCE │
│ │
└────────────┘
IB LOW

After the initial balance forms, observe whether price:

  • Remains inside the range.

  • Extends above it.

  • Extends below it.

  • Breaks out and returns.

  • Establishes acceptance outside it.

A breakout alone does not confirm a trend.

CHAPTER 09Acceptance and Rejection

9.1 Acceptance

Acceptance occurs when the market spends sufficient time and conducts sufficient business at a price region.

Evidence can include:

  • Repeated trading.

  • Increasing volume.

  • Sustained price presence.

  • Developing value.

  • Multiple rotations.

Example:

text

PREVIOUS VALUE

┌───────┐
│ │
└───────┘
\
\
NEW PRICE
┌────────┐
│ ↗ ↘ │
│ ↖ ↗ │
└────────┘

ACCEPTANCE

The market has developed a new area of business.

9.2 Rejection

Rejection occurs when price explores an area but fails to establish sustained participation.

Evidence can include:

  • Quick movement away.

  • Failure to maintain prices.

  • Lack of developing volume.

  • Sharp response from the tested area.

text

HIGH
X
/
/
┌──────────┐
│ VALUE │
│ │
└──────────┘

REJECTION

9.3 The most important question

Do not ask only:

"Did price break the level?"

Ask:

"Did the market accept the price beyond the level?"

That distinction is central to AMT.

CHAPTER 10Market Profile Shapes

10.1 D-shaped profile

A relatively balanced distribution.

text

███
█████
███████
█████
███

Interpretation:

  • Rotational activity.

  • Two-sided participation.

  • Value concentrated around the middle.

10.2 P-shaped profile

text

█████
███
██
██

Can develop after upward price movement followed by acceptance near higher prices.

It is not automatically bullish.

10.3 b-shaped profile

text

██
██

█████
███████

Can develop after downward price movement followed by acceptance at lower prices.

It is not automatically bearish.

10.4 Trend profile

text

██
██
██
██
██
██
██

A narrow, elongated distribution can reflect directional activity.

Always examine the session context and the development of value.

CHAPTER 11Initiative and Responsive Activity

11.1 Initiative buyers

Participants who actively pursue higher prices.

They may be responsible for:

  • Upward range extension.

  • Breakouts.

  • Higher developing value.

  • Sustained upward movement.

11.2 Initiative sellers

Participants who actively pursue lower prices.

They may contribute to:

  • Downward range extension.

  • Breakdown.

  • Lower developing value.

  • Sustained downward movement.

11.3 Responsive buyers

Participants who become active at relatively lower prices and oppose further downside.

11.4 Responsive sellers

Participants who become active at relatively higher prices and oppose further upside.

Comparison

Initiative Responsive
Drives price away from value Opposes movement away from value
Seeks new prices Defends or responds to existing prices
Can produce trends Can produce rotations

A trader should understand which type of activity appears to be controlling the current auction.

CHAPTER 12Failed Auctions

A failed auction occurs when the market attempts to explore new prices but cannot maintain that exploration.

Example:

text

BREAKOUT
↑
X
/ \
/ \
┌─────────────┐
│ BALANCE │
│ │
└─────────────┘
↓
RETURN TO VALUE

A failed upside auction can indicate that buyers were unable to establish acceptance at higher prices.

A failed downside auction can indicate that sellers were unable to establish acceptance at lower prices.

A useful analysis sequence:

  1. Identify the previous balance.

  2. Observe the breakout.

  3. Watch for sustained participation.

  4. Determine whether price returns into value.

  5. Observe whether the opposite side becomes active.

A failed auction is a context, not an automatic reversal signal.

CHAPTER 13Single Prints and Excess

13.1 Single prints

Single prints are TPO price levels visited during only one time bracket within the selected profile.

They can indicate rapid movement through an area.

They often appear during directional activity.

13.2 Excess

Excess refers to a clearly rejected auction extreme, often represented by a tail of single prints.

A buying tail can form at a low.

A selling tail can form at a high.

13.3 Poor high and poor low

A poor high or poor low is an extreme without a clear excess structure.

It can suggest that the auction did not finish with a decisive rejection.

These levels may later be revisited and repaired.

However, none of these structures guarantees a future price movement.

CHAPTER 14Composite Profiles

A composite profile combines multiple sessions into one larger distribution.

Instead of studying only today's auction, it allows the trader to examine several days or weeks of activity.

Important components:

  • Composite POC.

  • Composite VAH.

  • Composite VAL.

  • Major HVNs.

  • Major LVNs.

  • Areas of overlapping value.

Why use composites?

Markets can establish important areas of acceptance over multiple sessions.

A single daily profile may not reveal the larger structure.

Composite profiles help identify broader balance areas and major historical reference levels.

CHAPTER 15Reading Market Context

Before considering any trade, answer these questions:

  1. Where is current price relative to yesterday's value?

  2. Is today's opening inside or outside previous value?

  3. Is the market inside a multi-day balance?

  4. Is value moving higher or lower?

  5. Is the Initial Balance being respected?

  6. Is the market accepting or rejecting new prices?

  7. Are buyers or sellers showing initiative?

  8. Where are the nearest major HVNs and LVNs?

  9. Is the current session rotational or directional?

  10. What would invalidate the current market interpretation?

Context comes before execution.

CHAPTER 16Practical Trading Scenarios

Scenario A: Opening inside previous value

The market opens inside the previous session's value area.

Possible interpretation:

The auction is opening in an area where trade was previously accepted.

Observe whether the market continues rotating or begins developing outside value.

Do not assume a range day simply because the open is inside value.

Scenario B: Opening above previous value

Possible interpretation:

The market is exploring higher prices.

Observe:

  • Whether previous VAH holds.

  • Whether price returns into previous value.

  • Whether higher prices attract participation.

  • Whether developing value migrates upward.

Scenario C: Opening below previous value

Possible interpretation:

The market is exploring lower prices.

Observe:

  • Whether previous VAL holds.

  • Whether price returns into value.

  • Whether lower prices attract sellers.

  • Whether value begins developing lower.

Scenario D: Breakout and acceptance

Price breaks above a balance area and continues trading there.

The market may be establishing higher value.

The important confirmation is sustained participation, not simply the initial breakout.

Scenario E: Breakout and rejection

Price breaks outside a balance area but quickly returns.

The auction may have failed to establish value outside the range.

Watch for a potential rotation back through the previous balance.

CHAPTER 17Building An AMT Trading Plan

A useful AMT trading plan has five stages.

Stage 1: Higher-timeframe context

Identify:

  • Weekly balance.

  • Daily balance.

  • Major composite levels.

  • Previous session value.

  • Important structural extremes.

Stage 2: Opening analysis

Record:

  • Opening price.

  • Previous VAH and VAL.

  • Previous POC.

  • Overnight high and low.

  • Initial Balance.

Stage 3: Auction interpretation

Determine:

  • Balance or imbalance?

  • Acceptance or rejection?

  • Initiative or responsive activity?

  • Developing value higher or lower?

Stage 4: Execution

Wait for a setup that agrees with the market context.

Define:

  • Entry condition.

  • Invalidation level.

  • Stop-loss.

  • Target.

  • Position size.

Stage 5: Review

Record whether your original auction interpretation was correct.

Do not judge the quality of a decision solely by whether it made money.

CHAPTER 18Risk Management

AMT does not remove trading risk.

Every trading idea must have a defined invalidation point.

Important principles:

  • Never assume a level must hold.

  • Do not increase position size to recover losses.

  • Avoid trading during unclear market conditions.

  • Account for commissions and slippage.

  • Reduce risk around major scheduled events when appropriate.

  • Use historical testing before trusting a setup.

Risk calculation

Position risk:

Position size × Stop distance × Value per point

Example:

Account balance: $10,000

Risk per trade: 0.5%

Maximum planned loss: $50

If the instrument's stop distance and contract value imply a $100 loss, the position is too large for that risk limit.

CHAPTER 19Common Mistakes

  1. Treating every POC as a guaranteed magnet.

  2. Assuming every breakout will continue.

  3. Assuming every return into value will traverse the entire range.

  4. Confusing Volume POC with TPO POC.

  5. Using the 70% value area as an exact mathematical law.

  6. Ignoring higher-timeframe context.

  7. Entering without a clear invalidation level.

  8. Treating every HVN as support or resistance.

  9. Assuming single prints must always be filled.

  10. Trading profile shapes without understanding how they developed.

Important note about probabilities

The frequently quoted 80% value-area rule is a trading heuristic, not a universal probability.

Results depend on the instrument, session definition, sample period, entry conditions and precise definition of acceptance.

A trader should independently test any probability before using it as a basis for risk.

CHAPTER 20Advanced Concepts

20.1 Developing POC

The developing POC changes as new volume or TPO activity accumulates.

Tracking its movement can help identify whether value is migrating.

20.2 Value migration

When successive profiles establish higher value areas, the market may be developing an upward shift in acceptance.

When value areas move lower, the opposite may be occurring.

20.3 Overnight inventory

Overnight inventory describes the positioning implied by price movement during the overnight session.

It provides context for the regular session open.

Observe whether overnight movement is maintained or unwound after the main session begins.

20.4 Double distribution

A double-distribution profile contains two distinct areas of activity separated by a relatively low-activity region.

It can reflect two separate phases of acceptance during one session.

20.5 Unfinished auction

An unfinished auction generally refers to an extreme that lacks the clear excess structure expected at a completed auction extreme.

It is a reference for future observation, not a guaranteed revisit.

CHAPTER 21Practical Exercises

Exercise 1: Identify the market state

Price spends several hours rotating inside a narrow range.

Volume accumulates near the center.

Question: Is this balance or imbalance?

Answer: Balance.

Exercise 2: Identify acceptance

Price breaks above VAH and continues trading above it. Volume builds and developing value moves higher.

Question: What is happening?

Answer: The market is showing evidence of acceptance at higher prices.

Exercise 3: Identify rejection

Price breaks below VAL but quickly returns into the previous value area.

Question: What should you investigate?

Answer: Whether the downside auction failed and whether the market is beginning to rotate back into value.

Exercise 4: TPO vs. Volume

A price level has many TPO letters but relatively low traded volume.

Question: What does this tell you?

Answer: Price spent considerable time there, but traded volume was relatively low. Time and volume are measuring different things.

Exercise 5: Build a market narrative

Given:

  • Previous session was balanced.

  • Today opens above VAH.

  • Price tests VAH.

  • Price holds above it.

  • Developing POC moves higher.

Question: What is the current auction suggesting?

Answer: Possible acceptance and upward value migration. The interpretation remains valid only while supporting evidence persists.

CHAPTER 22Daily Trading Checklist

Before the session

  • Mark previous VAH.

  • Mark previous VAL.

  • Mark previous POC.

  • Mark overnight high and low.

  • Identify major composite levels.

  • Check scheduled economic events.

  • Determine higher-timeframe context.

During the session

  • Identify the Initial Balance.

  • Monitor developing value.

  • Observe initiative and responsive activity.

  • Look for acceptance and rejection.

  • Identify failed auctions.

  • Monitor HVNs and LVNs.

  • Avoid forcing trades in unclear conditions.

After the session

  • Save the chart.

  • Record the day's market structure.

  • Compare initial and final value.

  • Review trading decisions.

  • Record mistakes.

  • Update the trading journal.

CHAPTER 23Complete AMT Glossary

Term Definition
AMT Auction Market Theory
POC Point of Control
VPOC Volume Point of Control
TPO Time Price Opportunity
VA Value Area
VAH Value Area High
VAL Value Area Low
HVN High Volume Node
LVN Low Volume Node
IB Initial Balance
RTH Regular Trading Hours
ETH Extended Trading Hours

Rejection Failure to sustain trade at a price area
Excess Clear rejection at an auction extreme

Responsive Activity opposing movement away from value
Composite Profile combining multiple sessions

Imbalance Directional auction

CHAPTER 24The AMT Mindset

The most important skill in Auction Market Theory is not memorizing profile terminology.

It is learning to interpret the auction as it develops.

A professional analysis should answer three questions:

1. Where is the market?

Identify current price relative to established value and important structural levels.

2. What is the market doing?

Determine whether the auction is balancing, trending, accepting or rejecting prices.

3. What would prove your interpretation wrong?

Identify the conditions that invalidate your market narrative.

The objective is not to predict every movement.

The objective is to understand market behavior, recognize changing conditions and manage risk when acting on a trading idea.

Remember: Context first. Auction second. Execution last.
