Volume Profile

Illustrated study guide, based on the Order Flow Labs lesson. The diagrams are conceptual teaching visuals, not live market data or signals.

Chapters · tap to jumpHow to use this guide1. What is Volume Profile?2. Value Area3. High Volume Nodes (HVNs)4. Low Volume Nodes (LVNs)5. Shelf and Ledge6. Composite Volume Profiles7. Session Volume Profiles8. Volume Footprint9. Practical reading sequenceSource and scope

PART 01How to use this guide

The diagrams are conceptual teaching visuals—not live market data, trading signals, or exact reproductions of the source page’s images. Read each profile as volume distributed horizontally across price levels.

Source: Order Flow Labs, “Volume Profile.” The source describes Volume Profile as a structural framework, not a standalone trading strategy.

PART 021. What is Volume Profile?

Volume Profile organizes traded volume horizontally by price instead of plotting it only across time. It helps show where the market facilitated the most and least trade during a selected period.

Volume is the number of shares or contracts exchanged. Aggregating that activity at price levels can reveal zones of stronger agreement and prices that were traversed with less participation.

In the lesson’s framing, higher-volume areas often correspond to value or agreement; lower-volume areas can reflect reduced participation and directional movement. These are structural observations—not guaranteed predictions.

PART 032. Value Area

The Value Area is the range containing approximately 70% of a session’s traded volume. It reflects the zone where buyers and sellers were most willing to transact and where trade was facilitated efficiently.

• Value Area High (VAH): upper boundary.
• Value Area Low (VAL): lower boundary.
• Point of Control (POC): price level with the greatest traded volume in the period, typically centered within the area.

When price remains inside value, activity is often rotational. A test of VAH or VAL may rotate back toward POC or develop into an imbalance. Trading outside value indicates comparatively reduced participation in the source’s explanation.

PART 043. High Volume Nodes (HVNs)

High Volume Nodes are price areas where substantial volume traded, suggesting strong agreement between buyers and sellers. Each HVN can be viewed as a prior area of value and contains its own local POC.

Trade inside an HVN is typically associated with balance and efficient facilitation. The node’s outer edges matter because they can define acceptance/rejection boundaries and decision points in an Auction Market Theory context.

PART 054. Low Volume Nodes (LVNs)

Low Volume Nodes are price areas with relatively little traded volume. They indicate limited agreement and often represent zones through which price moved quickly.

The lesson describes LVNs as typically imbalanced areas with little structural support or resistance. Price may reject quickly or travel through the LVN toward higher-participation areas. They can act as transition zones between value areas; the response depends on whether participation returns.

PART 065. Shelf and Ledge

A shelf is a price area where volume expands and stabilizes, suggesting increased acceptance and trade facilitation. When revisited, such an area may slow price or encourage rotation.

A ledge is the outer edge of a shelf, where volume drops off quickly. The source says there is no functional distinction beyond this boundary relationship: the ledge marks the transition from acceptance toward rejection.

PART 076. Composite Volume Profiles

A Composite Volume Profile combines volume from multiple sessions into one profile. It gives a broader structural view of participation and areas of balance or imbalance, while smoothing some short-term noise.

The lesson lists common composite windows of 5, 7, 30, 90, 180, and 365 days. Shorter composites tend to emphasize recent structure; longer ones can capture more established value. Choose the period to fit the timeframe and context being analyzed.

PART 087. Session Volume Profiles

Session profiles organize volume within defined trading sessions, allowing participation and value to be compared across the trading day.

The source defines Overnight (ON) as 18:00–09:30 and Regular Trading Hours (RTH) as 09:30–16:00. Prior day, week, and month profiles are also used as historical references.

Comparing session profiles can help track day-to-day changes in structure and identify prior POCs, value areas, and extremes that price may respond to when revisited.

PART 098. Volume Footprint

A Volume Footprint (also called Candlestick Volume Profile in the lesson) displays traded volume inside each individual candle, at each price level. Instead of treating a candle as an empty price bar, it exposes how activity was distributed as price moved.

Footprints can reveal concentrated participation, aggressive buying or selling, and price levels that attracted or rejected volume. The lesson describes higher timeframes as useful for opportunity zones and structural acceptance, while lower timeframes can support more precise execution and short-term decisions.

PART 109. Practical reading sequence

  1. Choose the profile scope first: composite, session, or an individual candle footprint.

  2. Locate the main volume concentrations (HVNs) and the thinner areas (LVNs).

  3. Mark the value area boundaries (VAH and VAL) and the POC for the selected period.

  4. Observe whether price is rotating within accepted value, testing an edge, or moving through a low-participation zone.

  5. Use these levels as structural context—not as a complete trading strategy or a guarantee of future behavior.

PART 11Source and scope

This guide follows the concepts and definitions in Order Flow Labs’ Volume Profile education page. Visuals are newly drawn conceptual diagrams and are not copied from the source. No additional claims about strategy performance or predictive certainty are made.

Source URL: https://orderflw.com/education/volume-profile

Trading Psychology

The Professional Trader’s Mindset: a complete masterclass on discipline, patience, execution and consistency, built for traders who use footprint pattern recognition, structured execution and risk management.

Parts · tap to jumpAbout this guidePART I · Understanding the trader's mindPART II · Uncertainty, probability and loss aversionPART III · Fear, greed, regret and emotional decision-makingPART IV · FOMO, missed opportunities and comparisonPART V · Revenge trading, tilt and emotional spiralsPART VI · Overtrading, boredom, impatience and waitingPART VII · Confidence, hesitation and self-doubtPART VIII · Footprint pattern recognition and psychologyPART IX · Process over outcomePART X · Risk management and drawdownsPART XI · Discipline and consistencyPART XII · The psychology of winning and losingPART XIII · Journaling and performance reviewPART XIV · The professional trading routinePART XV · Practical psychological trainingPART XVI · The professional trader's rulebookAPPENDIX A · A One-Page Session CardAPPENDIX B · Simple Trade Journal TemplateAPPENDIX C · Weekly Review TemplateScope

STARTAbout this guide

This guide combines the requested themes of trading psychology into one practical learning resource. It is written for a futures trader whose decisions are based on recognizing recurring Footprint patterns and evaluating them in context. It deliberately does not teach DOM operation or make DOM reading a prerequisite. The central idea is simple: technical recognition and psychological execution are separate skills. A trader may recognize a valid pattern yet hesitate, chase, overtrade, move a stop or become attached to a directional opinion. This guide focuses on building the habits that help keep execution aligned with a tested plan.

ImportantA valid setup can lose. A poor trade can win. Evaluate the quality of the decision separately from the financial outcome.

How to use this guide

  • Read the chapters in order once to understand the complete framework.
  • Choose one behavioural weakness at a time instead of trying to fix everything at once.
  • Use the checklists and journal prompts during simulated or appropriately sized trading.
  • Evaluate patterns over a meaningful sample; do not draw conclusions from a handful of trades.
  • Adapt all risk limits to your tested strategy, account size and any prop-firm rules that apply.

PART IUnderstanding the trader's mind

1. Knowing what to do versus doing it

One of the hardest parts of trading is the gap between knowledge and behaviour. Away from the market, a trader can calmly explain the setup, entry, invalidation and risk. During a live position, money is at risk and the same decisions can feel completely different.

The analytical side

  • Builds the trading plan and defines setups.
  • Reviews historical examples and identifies recurring conditions.
  • Sets entry criteria, invalidation and risk before execution.
  • Reviews results over a meaningful sample.

The reactive side

  • Wants to avoid the discomfort of a loss.
  • Wants to recover after a losing trade.
  • Fears missing a fast move.
  • May take action simply to escape boredom or uncertainty.
The objectiveThe goal is not to eliminate emotion. It is to notice emotion without allowing it to rewrite the rules. Repetition builds the ability to follow a calm, predefined process under pressure.

2. Trading is a probabilistic activity

A good trade does not have to win, and a bad trade can sometimes make money. Markets are uncertain. A single outcome cannot tell you whether a decision was sound.

A simple expectancy example

Imagine a hypothetical strategy with 45 winners averaging +2R and 55 losers averaging −1R. Its expectancy before costs is (0.45 × 2R) − (0.55 × 1R) = +0.35R per trade. It can have positive expectancy while losing more often than it wins.

Think in series

  • Evaluate comparable trades over a meaningful sample.
  • Do not judge the strategy from one or two outcomes.
  • Keep execution quality separate from the P&L result.
  • Include commissions, slippage and realistic execution in performance analysis.
A professional questionInstead of asking, “Will this trade win?”, ask, “Does this opportunity meet my tested conditions, and is the risk acceptable?”

3. Accepting uncertainty

The market does not know your entry price, daily target or previous losses. It has no obligation to validate your opinion. When a trader becomes attached to a prediction, new evidence is often interpreted as a reason to defend the original view.

Recognize attachment

  • You keep repeating that price must reverse at a particular level.
  • You explain away evidence that contradicts your idea.
  • You widen the stop because you do not want the trade thesis to fail.
  • You treat being wrong as a personal failure.

Respond objectively

Define in advance what would invalidate the idea. If that condition occurs, accept it. Changing your interpretation when evidence changes is not weakness; it is disciplined adaptation.

PART IIUncertainty, probability and loss aversion

4. Why money changes behaviour

A historical chart can be studied without financial pressure. A live trade has immediate consequences, and that pressure can change attention, confidence and execution.

Two versions of the same setup

In replay, you may identify a pattern calmly. Live, you may hesitate because the previous trade lost, or enter too early because you fear the move will disappear. The market picture may be similar while your internal state is different.

Questions before execution

  • Would I take this setup if I had not just won or lost?
  • Am I acting because the pattern is valid, or because I feel pressure?
  • Is the risk acceptable before I enter?
  • Can I accept the planned loss without changing the stop?

Reduce pressure through preparation

Predefine the setup, risk, invalidation and management rules. The fewer important decisions left to improvise during a fast market, the less room there is for emotional bargaining.

5. Loss aversion

Loss aversion is the tendency to experience losses more strongly than equivalent gains. In trading it can lead to holding losers, taking profits too early and avoiding valid setups after a losing streak.

Holding a losing trade

A trader refuses to close because realizing the loss feels painful. They begin hoping price returns to entry, even though the original invalidation condition has been reached.

Taking profits too early

The trader focuses on protecting unrealized profit rather than following the planned exit. A normal retracement feels like a threat.

Avoiding valid setups

After losses, the trader becomes excessively cautious and rejects trades that still meet the strategy's criteria.

Reframe the lossA predefined loss is a business cost, not a verdict on your ability. The aim is to keep that cost controlled and consistent with the tested plan.

6. The discomfort of being wrong

Many traders do not merely dislike losing money; they dislike the feeling of having made an incorrect judgment. This can cause them to defend a position long after the evidence has changed.

Separate identity from a trade

  • A losing trade does not mean you are unintelligent.
  • A winning trade does not prove you are exceptional.
  • Your job is to make decisions under uncertainty, not to be right every time.

Use invalidation as protection

A clear invalidation point allows you to admit that the current idea is no longer valid without turning the decision into an argument with yourself.

PART IIIFear, greed, regret and emotional decision-making

7. Fear and the execution problem

Fear appears as fear of losing, fear of giving back profits and fear after a losing streak. It may cause a trader to hesitate, exit early, skip valid entries or demand extra confirmation that was never part of the strategy.

Fear of losing

The trader recognizes a valid setup but cannot accept the possibility of a loss. They wait for certainty that does not exist.

Fear of giving back profit

The trader closes a position prematurely because unrealized profit feels like money already owned.

Fear after a losing streak

The trader questions every signal, changes rules impulsively or stops trusting a tested setup.

Practical response

Define entry, invalidation, risk and management before the trade. If the setup is valid and risk is acceptable, the decision should be based on the plan—not on a demand to feel completely comfortable.

8. Greed and overconfidence

Greed is not only wanting more money. It can be the urge to capture every move, take another trade immediately after a win or increase size because the trader feels unusually capable.

Winning streak danger

  • Confidence rises after several winners.
  • Selectivity may decline.
  • The trader may increase size without evidence.
  • A weaker setup begins to look acceptable.
Keep confidence groundedPosition size should follow predefined risk rules, not excitement. Previous wins do not make the next trade more likely to succeed.

9. Regret and hindsight bias

A missed trade can create the illusion that the opportunity was obvious and easy. After seeing the market move, a trader may forget the uncertainty that existed before the move.

The regret loop

You skip a setup, price moves in the expected direction, and you tell yourself you knew it would happen. You then feel compelled to catch the next move, even if it is lower quality.

A missed trade is not a loss

You cannot lose money on a trade you did not enter. Review whether the decision was correct based on the information available at the time, not on what became obvious afterwards.

10. Emotional decision-making

Emotions are signals, not instructions. Frustration may signal that expectations were unrealistic. Fear may signal that risk is too large. Excitement may signal that confidence is turning into impulsiveness.

Name the emotion

  • “I am frustrated because I missed the entry.”
  • “I am anxious because the position is too large for me.”
  • “I am excited after a winning streak.”
Choose a rule-based responseOnce the emotion is named, decide what your plan requires. You may need to wait, reduce exposure, take a break or finish the session.

PART IVFOMO, missed opportunities and comparison

11. Fear of missing out

FOMO is the fear that an opportunity will disappear without you. It is especially relevant to fast-moving futures markets, where a recognizable pattern may develop and resolve quickly.

The three stages

  • Observation: you notice a possible opportunity.
  • Attachment: you begin imagining the profit and feel that this specific trade must be yours.
  • Chasing: the planned entry is gone, but you enter anyway.

Why chasing is dangerous

  • The entry is worse than planned.
  • The invalidation may no longer be clear.
  • The reward-to-risk profile may have deteriorated.
  • The trade is motivated by urgency rather than criteria.

The missed-trade rule

If the planned entry is no longer available, the opportunity may be gone. Do not move the goalposts simply because the original idea was correct.

12. Stop comparing your performance

Social media often displays winning trades, large payouts and impressive daily results without showing the full distribution of losses, risk, account history or execution quality.

Comparison creates pressure

You may feel behind and begin forcing trades to match another person's apparent results.

Use your own evidence

  • Are you respecting stops more often?
  • Are impulsive entries decreasing?
  • Are you recognizing your setups more consistently?
  • Is your execution score improving?
A better benchmarkCompare your current behaviour with your own previous behaviour. Your journal is more useful than another trader's highlight reel.

13. Missed opportunities: selectivity or hesitation?

Not every missed trade is a mistake. Sometimes rejecting a setup is exactly the right decision. Other times, fear prevents execution even though all conditions are satisfied.

Classify the miss

  • Correctly rejected: the setup was incomplete or invalid.
  • No confirmation: the pattern never met the entry rule.
  • Hesitation: the setup was valid but fear stopped execution.
  • Distraction: attention was elsewhere.
  • Emotional carryover: a previous trade affected the decision.

Review without hindsight

Record the conditions as they appeared at the time. Do not classify a missed trade as a mistake merely because price later moved in the expected direction.

PART VRevenge trading, tilt and emotional spirals

14. Revenge trading

Revenge trading occurs when the main motivation for another position is to recover money lost on a previous trade. The trader stops evaluating the next opportunity independently.

Typical progression

  • A valid trade loses.
  • Frustration creates a need to recover.
  • A weaker setup is accepted.
  • Another loss increases emotional pressure.
  • Size or frequency may increase in an attempt to get back to breakeven.

Break the cycle

  • Use a predefined break after a specified number of losses.
  • Never increase size to recover.
  • Respect the daily loss limit.
  • If you are focused on recovering money, stop and reassess.
  • End the session if calm execution does not return.
A better recovery goalAfter a losing session, aim to recover your discipline—not your money. The next session does not have to be profitable to be successful.

15. Tilt: recognizing loss of control

Tilt is a state in which emotional pressure begins to distort decisions. A trader may still believe they are analysing objectively while their behaviour becomes impulsive.

Physical warning signs

  • Raised heart rate or shallow breathing.
  • Tension in the shoulders or jaw.
  • Restlessness and difficulty concentrating.

Behavioural warning signs

  • Clicking faster than usual.
  • Entering before confirmation.
  • Moving stops impulsively.
  • Watching P&L constantly.
  • Feeling angry when price moves without you.
  • Taking trades you would normally reject.

Emergency protocol

  • Stop looking for entries.
  • Step away from the screen.
  • Take slow breaths and identify the trigger.
  • Review daily risk limits.
  • Resume only if your predefined conditions for continuing are satisfied.

16. Build a stop-trading rule

The ability to stop is part of risk management. Do not leave the decision to continue entirely to the emotional state that may be causing the problem.

Predefine stopping conditions

  • Maximum daily loss.
  • Maximum number of trades, if appropriate for your plan.
  • A required break after consecutive losses.
  • A clear rule for emotional impairment.
  • A rule for ending after a planned objective or session window.

Do not negotiate in the moment

The limits should be decided while calm. If a stopping condition is reached, follow it without bargaining.

PART VIOvertrading, boredom, impatience and waiting

17. Overtrading

Overtrading is not simply taking a large number of trades. It is taking trades that do not meet the strategy's requirements. A small number of impulsive entries can be overtrading; several valid setups need not be.

Common causes

  • Boredom after a quiet period.
  • Impatience with a developing pattern.
  • Greed after a profitable trade.
  • Frustration after a loss.
  • No defined session window or stopping conditions.

Quality over quantity

Measure the proportion of trades that satisfy your complete criteria. Do not increase trade count just to feel productive.

18. Boredom and the need for action

Watching a market for a long time without a setup can feel unproductive. This can lead to taking a trade simply to make something happen.

Reframe inactivity

  • Waiting protects capital.
  • Waiting preserves selectivity.
  • Waiting allows conditions to develop.
  • Waiting reduces unnecessary mental fatigue.
A professional habitTreat no-trade sessions as legitimate outcomes. If the market does not offer your setup, standing aside is a valid decision.

19. Patience versus hesitation

Patience means waiting until predefined conditions are satisfied. Hesitation means refusing to execute after they are satisfied because the trader fears the outcome.

Decision guide

  • Conditions incomplete: wait.
  • Conditions satisfied but fear is present: recognize the fear and follow the tested plan if risk is acceptable.
  • Entry has passed: accept the missed opportunity.
  • Setup invalidated: do not force it.

Avoid both extremes

The goal is not to trade aggressively or defensively. It is to trade consistently according to tested criteria.

20. Analysis paralysis

More information does not always create better decisions. Switching interpretations repeatedly or demanding endless confirmation can make execution impossible.

Use a decision hierarchy

  • Is the market context suitable?
  • Is the price location relevant to the setup?
  • Is the predefined pattern developing?
  • Is the required confirmation present?
  • Is risk acceptable?
  • Is the setup still valid?

Keep the hierarchy stable

Do not add new criteria during a live trade simply because you feel uncertain. Review and improve the criteria outside the session.

PART VIIConfidence, hesitation and self-doubt

21. Build confidence from evidence

Useful confidence is grounded in knowledge, repetition, statistical evidence and execution. It is not the same as feeling certain that the next trade will win.

Four foundations

  • Knowledge: understand the exact setup and its conditions.
  • Repetition: study it across different sessions and market conditions.
  • Evidence: collect enough observations to evaluate performance after costs.
  • Execution: demonstrate that you can follow the plan live.

Avoid false confidence

A few winners do not prove an edge. A few losers do not disprove one. Confidence should reflect the quality of your evidence and the consistency of your execution.

22. Fear of pressing the button

A trader may identify a valid setup, define risk and still hesitate. Often the mind has shifted from evaluating the decision to imagining the pain of a possible loss.

Training exercise

  • Use replay or simulation to practise identifying the exact setup.
  • Write down entry and invalidation conditions.
  • Define risk before execution.
  • Record whether you followed the rule.
  • Review hesitation separately from the trade outcome.

Do not force every trade

The objective is not to enter every opportunity. It is to make a consistent decision when the complete criteria are present and the risk is acceptable.

23. Confidence after consecutive losses

A losing streak can cause a trader to change the strategy after every unsuccessful trade. Before changing anything, identify whether the issue is normal variance, execution deterioration or a genuine change in strategy performance.

Normal variance

Trades followed the strategy, but outcomes were unfavourable. Continue evaluating only if risk limits remain intact and the sample supports the approach.

Execution deterioration

You took lower-quality entries, ignored stops or traded emotionally. Reduce exposure or pause, then address the behavioural errors.

Strategy deterioration

Evidence suggests the strategy's performance or market conditions have changed. Conduct a structured review rather than making an emotional adjustment.

PART VIIIFootprint pattern recognition and psychology

24. Keep the focus on pattern recognition

For a Footprint-based trader, the goal is to recognize recurring market behaviours and assess whether the current context resembles situations covered by the trading plan. This guide focuses on that decision process, not DOM operation.

Pattern recognition should be structured

  • The setup has predefined criteria.
  • The location is relevant.
  • The conditions resemble studied examples.
  • Required confirmation is present.
  • The invalidation point is clear.

Pattern imagination

  • You recognize only one part of the setup.
  • You ignore conflicting evidence.
  • You enter because the market is moving quickly.
  • You modify criteria to justify an entry.
  • You interpret every observation in favour of an existing bias.
The key distinctionA setup is defined by its complete criteria, not by one familiar feature.

25. Confirmation bias

Confirmation bias is the tendency to seek information that supports an existing belief while ignoring contradictory evidence. A trader with a bullish bias may focus on signs of buying and overlook evidence that the idea is failing.

Challenge the idea

  • What evidence supports this trade?
  • What evidence contradicts it?
  • What would prove my interpretation wrong?
  • Am I seeing the complete pattern or only the part I want to see?
  • Would I take this setup without an existing directional bias?

Neutral observation

Do not defend a prediction. Evaluate whether current evidence satisfies the plan.

26. Attachment to a familiar pattern

A pattern that has worked well historically can become emotionally attractive. Familiarity may turn into overconfidence, causing the trader to take it in conditions where it has not been validated.

Watch for context drift

  • Similar visual structure in a different location.
  • Similar activity without required confirmation.
  • Conditions excluded from the tested strategy.
  • An entry motivated by memory of a previous winner.
RuleNever trade a pattern simply because it looks familiar. Trade it because the complete conditions are satisfied.

27. Trust the process, not the prediction

Pattern recognition should identify potential opportunities, not predict with certainty what price must do. A trader can form a directional idea, observe that conditions are no longer valid and stand aside.

Flexible thinking

  • A bullish idea can be invalidated.
  • A bearish idea can be invalidated.
  • No-trade is a valid decision.
  • Changing your interpretation when evidence changes is disciplined, not weak.

Avoid ego-driven analysis

Your goal is not to prove that your first interpretation was correct. Your goal is to respond to the market using a consistent method.

PART IXProcess over outcome

28. A winning trade can be a bad trade

A trade that makes money after an impulsive entry, undefined risk and a moved stop may be financially positive but procedurally poor. A trade that loses after a valid setup and correct risk management may be a process success.

Evaluate two dimensions

  • Was the setup valid and was execution correct?
  • Did the trade make or lose money?

Four possible outcomes

  • Correct execution + win: good process and positive outcome.
  • Correct execution + loss: good process and negative outcome.
  • Incorrect execution + win: poor process and positive outcome.
  • Incorrect execution + loss: poor process and negative outcome.

Reward the right behaviour

If you reward only profitable outcomes, you may reinforce bad habits. Evaluate whether you followed the plan independently of the P&L.;

29. Process goals instead of daily profit pressure

A fixed daily profit target can encourage a trader to lower standards when the market does not offer opportunities. Financial goals can become pressure to trade rather than a measure of a sound process.

Replace outcome demands

  • Instead of “I must make a fixed amount,” use “I will take only my predefined setups.”
  • Instead of “I must finish green,” use “I will respect risk limits.”
  • Instead of “I need to recover,” use “I will evaluate the next setup independently.”

What you control

You cannot force the market to provide opportunities. You can control how you participate.

30. A personal execution score

A simple score can help separate process quality from financial performance. For each trade, award one point for each item that was satisfied.

Five-point score

  • The setup met the complete criteria.
  • The entry followed the plan.
  • Risk was predefined.
  • The stop and exit rules were respected.
  • Management followed the plan.

Interpretation

A 5/5 losing trade can be a process success. A 1/5 winning trade is not a model to repeat. Track scores over time and compare them with results.

PART XRisk management and drawdowns

31. Risk management protects your psychology

Risk management is not only financial. Oversized positions can make normal price movement feel threatening, causing early exits, stop interference and poor decisions.

Risk rules

  • Calculate risk before entry.
  • Never increase size to recover.
  • Do not move a stop farther away because the loss is uncomfortable.
  • Respect daily and account-level limits.
  • Avoid trading when emotionally compromised.
  • Evaluate risk across a series of trades.

Size and emotional comfort

If the planned loss would seriously affect your finances or ability to think clearly, the risk may be too large. Adjust exposure to your tested plan and account constraints.

32. Understanding drawdowns

A drawdown is a decline from a previous equity high. Drawdowns can be part of a strategy's normal distribution, but they can also reveal execution or strategy problems.

Normal variance

Trades followed the plan, but outcomes were unfavourable. Evaluate over a suitable sample while respecting risk limits.

Execution problem

You deviated from the plan. Identify the behaviour and correct it before increasing exposure.

Strategy problem

The evidence suggests the edge or market conditions have changed. Review the data and assumptions objectively.

Do not assume

Do not automatically call every drawdown normal variance, and do not assume every drawdown means the strategy is broken.

33. Do not trade to recover your account

When a trader focuses on recovering a specific amount, attention shifts away from the setup and toward the account balance. This can create larger size, lower standards and urgency.

Reset the objective

  • Do not calculate how many points are needed to get back to breakeven.
  • Do not increase size because normal trades feel too small.
  • Do not treat the next setup as a recovery opportunity.
  • Return to the normal process and risk rules.
The right recoveryRecover disciplined behaviour first. A profitable next session is not required to demonstrate improvement.

PART XIDiscipline and consistency

34. Discipline is trained

Discipline develops through repeated behaviour. Every time you reject an invalid setup, respect a stop or accept a missed trade without chasing, you practise the behaviour you want to make habitual.

Build one rule at a time

  • Start with one non-negotiable rule.
  • Track compliance honestly.
  • Review what made the rule difficult.
  • Add another rule only after the first becomes more consistent.

Examples

  • No entry without complete confirmation.
  • No chasing missed setups.
  • No size increase after a loss.
  • No trading outside the planned session.
  • Journal after each session.

35. Self-awareness and self-control

Self-awareness is recognizing an impulse or emotional trigger. Self-control is choosing not to act on it automatically. Both are necessary.

Example

Self-awareness: “I feel impatient because the market has been quiet.” Self-control: “Boredom is not a setup, so I will wait.”

Daily reflection

  • Which emotion appeared most strongly?
  • What triggered it?
  • How did it influence my behaviour?
  • Did I notice it in real time?
  • What rule should guide my response next time?

36. Consistency over intensity

Constantly changing strategies, adding indicators or watching endless educational content can create the feeling of progress without improving execution. Consistency comes from repeatedly applying a clear, tested process and reviewing it honestly.

Small improvements compound

  • One fewer impulsive entry.
  • One correctly respected stop.
  • One missed move not chased.
  • One valid setup executed according to plan.
  • One recurring mistake identified and corrected.

PART XIIThe psychology of winning and losing

37. Handling losing days

A losing day is one observation, not a definition of your ability. The danger is carrying frustration into the next session or trying to prove yourself through more aggressive trading.

Review objectively

  • Did I follow my rules?
  • Were the setups valid?
  • Was risk appropriate?
  • Did I make emotional decisions?
  • Is the loss within the strategy's expected behaviour?

Close the session mentally

Extract the lesson and stop replaying every tick. Do not carry yesterday's emotional state into today's decisions.

38. Handling winning days

Winning can produce overconfidence, lower selectivity and unnecessary additional trades. A strong session is a reason to preserve discipline, not abandon it.

Protect the process

  • Do not increase size because you feel confident.
  • Do not keep trading simply because you are winning.
  • Respect the planned session and stopping conditions.
  • Record execution quality, not only profit.

39. Emotional neutrality

Emotional neutrality does not mean having no feelings. It means experiencing feelings without allowing them to control execution.

Examples

  • Feel nervous but follow the risk plan.
  • Feel disappointed but accept the loss.
  • Feel excited but avoid overtrading.
  • Feel frustrated about a missed move but wait for the next valid setup.

Professional objective

You do not need to eliminate emotions. You need to prevent them from making your trading decisions.

PART XIIIJournaling and performance review

40. The journal as a performance laboratory

A useful trading journal records decisions, context, emotions and execution—not only entries, exits and profit. It can reveal patterns that are difficult to notice in the moment.

What a journal may reveal

  • Worst trades happen after missed opportunities.
  • Impatience rises after long periods without a setup.
  • Profits are taken early after consecutive losses.
  • Execution quality changes during different parts of the session.
  • Overconfidence follows a winning streak.
The purposeTurn experiences into evidence. Avoid using the journal as a place to punish yourself.

41. What to record for each trade

Use a consistent template so trades can be compared later.

Trade record

  • Date and time.
  • Instrument and contract.
  • Setup name and criteria.
  • Market context and relevant location.
  • Entry, planned stop and exit.
  • Initial risk and result in R.
  • Confirmation conditions present.
  • Emotion before, during and after.
  • Execution score and lesson.

Keep records objective

Write what you observed and what you did. Avoid vague labels such as “bad feeling” without explaining the trigger.

42. Journal missed opportunities

Record valid opportunities that were not taken. This helps distinguish healthy selectivity from hesitation.

Classify each missed opportunity

  • Correctly rejected.
  • Confirmation never appeared.
  • Missed due to hesitation.
  • Missed due to distraction.
  • Missed due to emotional carryover.

Avoid hindsight bias

Judge the decision based on the information available at the time, not on the eventual market move.

43. Weekly psychological review

At the end of each week, review behaviour across the full sample.

Weekly questions

  • How many trades followed the plan?
  • How many were impulsive?
  • How many valid setups were missed?
  • Did I experience FOMO or revenge trading?
  • Did I respect stops and risk limits?
  • What was my most common emotional trigger?
  • What one behaviour will I improve next week?
FocusChoose one recurring weakness. Trying to fix everything at once makes it harder to measure progress.

PART XIVThe professional trading routine

44. Before the session

Psychological preparation starts before the first potential entry. Arrive with a plan rather than an expectation that the market must provide a trade.

Preparation checklist

  • Review the previous journal entry.
  • Read your setup and risk rules.
  • Identify the relevant market context.
  • Define session and daily risk limits.
  • Set stopping conditions.
  • Check whether you are rested and focused.

If you are not ready

If tired, distracted or emotionally overwhelmed, consider reducing exposure or not trading. Your mental condition is part of the trading environment.

45. During the session

Use the same decision sequence each time a potential pattern appears.

Execution sequence

  • Observe the market and context.
  • Check whether the location is relevant.
  • Identify whether the predefined pattern is developing.
  • Wait for required confirmation.
  • Define risk and invalidation.
  • Execute only if the setup remains valid.

After entry

  • Avoid unnecessary interference.
  • Respect exit conditions.
  • Do not let unrealized P&L become the only focus.
  • Do not invent reasons to stay in a trade.
  • Accept uncertainty.

After exit

Record the result and emotional state, evaluate execution, then move on.

46. After the session

Review the decisions you made, not only the amount of money earned or lost.

Post-session questions

  • Was I patient?
  • Did I force a trade?
  • Did I follow entry conditions?
  • Was I attached to a direction?
  • Did I chase any movement?
  • Did I stop when required?

Close the loop

Extract the lesson and finish the review. Replaying the session emotionally for hours is not the same as learning from it.

PART XVPractical psychological training

47. The 20-session discipline challenge

Choose one behavioural rule and track it for 20 sessions. For example: “I will not enter without my complete predefined setup.” Mark a session complete only after honestly evaluating whether you followed the rule.

Suggested progression

  • Sessions 1–5: identify the moments when the rule is hardest to follow.
  • Sessions 6–10: practise pausing when the trigger appears.
  • Sessions 11–15: review mistakes and refine the environment or routine.
  • Sessions 16–20: assess consistency and decide whether the habit is stable enough to build on.

Do not grade by P&L

The challenge measures compliance, not whether the sessions were profitable.

48. The emotional pause

Before entering, take a short pause and ask: Am I calm? Am I patient? Is the setup valid? Am I trying to recover something? Am I chasing? Is risk acceptable? If you cannot answer honestly, reassess rather than rush.

PurposeA pause can interrupt automatic behaviour and create space for a deliberate decision. It does not replace objective setup criteria.

49. The missed-opportunity study

For ten sessions, record every valid opportunity you observe but do not take. Classify it as correctly rejected, incomplete confirmation, hesitation, distraction or emotional carryover.

What to learn

  • Are you too selective or appropriately selective?
  • Do you hesitate after losses?
  • Do you miss setups because your rules are unclear?
  • Do you chase after missing an entry?

Review

Compare the opportunity with your predefined criteria at the time. Do not use the later price move as the only measure.

50. Emotional trigger mapping

At the end of each session, identify the strongest emotion, its trigger and the response you chose.

Examples

  • Fear after losses → follow predefined risk and avoid changing the stop.
  • Greed after wins → maintain normal size and selectivity.
  • FOMO during a fast move → reject late entries.
  • Frustration after a missed opportunity → wait for another setup.
  • Boredom in a quiet session → accept inactivity.
  • Overconfidence after profits → keep the same criteria.
Long-term aimRecognize your most common triggers early enough to respond deliberately.

PART XVIThe professional trader's rulebook

51. Twenty non-negotiable rules

These rules are a starting framework. Adapt them to your tested strategy and account rules, then keep them visible during the session.

Before trading

  • I will not trade simply because I want to make money.
  • I will know my risk before entering.
  • I will understand my predefined setups.
  • I will not trade when my emotional state makes disciplined execution unlikely.
  • I will prepare instead of improvising.

During trading

  • I will take only setups that meet my criteria.
  • I will not chase missed opportunities.
  • I will not enter because of boredom.
  • I will not increase size to recover a loss.
  • I will not move my stop farther away to avoid accepting a loss.
  • I will not let a previous trade determine the validity of the next setup.
  • I will accept that a valid trade can lose.
  • I will not confuse a profitable mistake with good execution.
  • I will stop when my predefined limits require it.

After trading

  • I will evaluate execution separately from P&L.;
  • I will journal my emotional state.
  • I will review missed opportunities.
  • I will identify recurring mistakes.
  • I will improve one behavioural weakness at a time.
  • I will not measure progress using a single trading day.

52. Pre-trade checklist

Before each entry, verify every item. A checklist is not a guarantee of profit; it is a safeguard against avoidable process errors.

Eight questions

  • Does this match one of my predefined setups?
  • Is the market context appropriate?
  • Are required confirmation conditions satisfied?
  • Am I entering at the planned location?
  • Is the invalidation point clear?
  • Is the risk within my limits?
  • Am I free of FOMO or revenge motivation?
  • Would I take this trade regardless of my previous trade's result?

If an answer is no

Pause and reassess. Do not lower the standard just to participate.

53. Post-session checklist

At the end of the session, answer these questions honestly.

Review questions

  • Did I respect my trading plan?
  • Did I recognize setups correctly?
  • Did I chase any opportunities?
  • Did I take unnecessary trades?
  • Did I manage risk correctly?
  • Did emotions influence execution?
  • What was my biggest mistake?
  • What was my best decision?
  • What will I improve next session?

Measure progress

The aim is to finish each session with a useful lesson, not necessarily a profit.

54. The trader you are becoming

Professional trading is not about being fearless or winning every day. It is about applying a rational, tested process when the outcome is uncertain. You will sometimes be wrong, late, frustrated or disappointed. The skill is to respond without abandoning your rules.

The professional mindset

  • Accept losses without revenge trading.
  • Wait without becoming impatient.
  • Miss opportunities without chasing.
  • Win without becoming overconfident.
  • Lose without questioning your identity.
  • Review mistakes without punishing yourself.
  • Keep risk controlled and decisions repeatable.
Final principleThe market will always offer uncertainty. Your job is to bring consistency.

APPENDIX AA One-Page Session Card

Before: Am I rested? What is my session plan? What are my risk and stopping limits? Which exact setups am I waiting for? During: Is the full setup present? Is the context appropriate? Is confirmation present? Is risk acceptable? Am I calm enough to execute? After: Did I follow the plan? What emotion appeared? Did I chase or overtrade? What is one lesson to carry forward?

No valid setup is a valid reason not to trade. A missed move is not a loss. A planned loss is not a personal failure.

SCOPEScope

Start here: what this is, in plain words

This is a simple day-trading method for NQ (Nasdaq futures). You do not need to learn everything in this guide to use it. Here is the whole method:

The 3 steps, every morning
  1. Mark the levels. Take yesterday’s high and keep its last two digits. Those digits change every day. Mark that ending every 100 points near price (the “digit levels”). Use the calculator in the “The digit levels” tab.
  2. Check each level on the volume profile. Only keep levels that sit at the edge of the weekly or daily balance. Skip the rest. This is 70% of your decision.
  3. Wait for the footprint to confirm. When price reaches a good level, look for absorption or stacked imbalances going your way. This is the other 30%. Then take one trade and stop for the day.

Which tabs to read, in order

WhenTabs
1. Read first (the method)Auction theory, Volume profile, The digit levels, Setups, Stops and size
2. ThenGEX and footprint, Gameplan and proof, Example
3. Optional knowledgeOrder flow toolkit, DOM. These help you understand why levels work. You do not trade from them
4. ToolsTemplates for your platform, Partners
5. Last, but importantProp-firm method, Mindset

The 100-point score

Use it to decide if a trade is worth taking.

PartWhat you checkPoints
Level (70)At a weekly balance edge or extreme25
Price within 2 points of the exact digit level15
Clear volume structure around it15
Between 9:30 and 11:00 ET, no news in the way15
Footprint (30)Absorption or exhaustion at the level10
Stacked imbalances your way10
Delta divergence or price fails to continue10

Suggested rule: trade only at 75 or more, and never if the level part is under 50. Test these numbers on your own data first.

Auction Market Theory (AMT) in one page

A market is an auction. Price moves to find the level where buyers and sellers both agree to trade a lot of volume. Go too high and buyers stop, sellers step in. Go too low and the reverse. That search is what you see on the chart.

Balance
Price rotates inside a range. Both sides trade, and prices inside are accepted as fair.
Imbalance
Price leaves the range and keeps going. One side is in control (a trend) until a new balance forms.
Acceptance
Price trades outside an area and stays there, building volume. The old edge becomes support or resistance.
Rejection
Price pokes outside and comes back fast. The move found no takers.
Initiative and responsive
Initiative traders push price out of balance. Responsive traders fade it back in.
Value area and POC
The value area holds about 70% of the volume. The POC (point of control) is the single price with the most volume.
Excess
A sharp tail where one side ran out. Often stops get swept, then price reverses.
Why this matters for your levels. A digit level is only interesting at an edge of a balance. There price has two honest outcomes: rejection (reversal, or sweep and reclaim) or acceptance (break and retest). In the middle of a balance price mostly chops, so skip it.

Deeper AMT: how to read the day

Open location
Open inside yesterday’s value area and the day tends to rotate (balance). Open outside it and the market is making a statement: either it accepts there and trends, or it fails and returns to value. Mark yesterday’s VAH, VAL and POC before 9:30.
Opening types
Open-drive (one-way from the bell, no pullback, strongest conviction), open-test-drive (tests one side, then drives the other), open-rejection-reverse (pushes out, fails, reverses), open-auction (rotates around the open, no commitment). Name the type by about 10:00 ET and let it set your stance: with the drive, or fade the failure.
Initial balance (IB)
The first hour’s high and low. A narrow IB hints at a trend day when it breaks. A wide IB usually means the range is already spent, so expect rotation inside it.
Day types
Normal (wide IB, stays inside), normal variation (one side extends), trend (narrow IB, one-way), double distribution (two value areas split by a thin LVN), neutral (both sides of the IB taken, closes mid-range). Only the trend and double-distribution days pay for holding; the rest pay for fast scalps.
The 80% rule
If price opens outside value, re-enters it, and then holds inside for two consecutive 30-minute periods, it travels to the opposite side of value about 80% of the time. That figure is a classic rule of thumb from Market Profile literature, not a guarantee. Test it on NQ before you trust it.
Single prints and poor highs
Single prints are fast, one-time-frame moves that often get revisited. A poor high or low (flat, no tail) signals unfinished business and often gets retested. A tail means excess, a real rejection.
Initiative vs responsive, in practice
Above yesterday’s value is “expensive”, so responsive sellers fade it unless initiative buyers prove they are accepted by holding there. Your digit level only matters when it lines up with one of these ideas.

AMT in practice: the full auction loop

Think of price as a shopkeeper testing what customers will pay. When most people accept a price, business is brisk (balance). When the price stops feeling fair to one side, that side either leaves or pushes, and price travels (imbalance). It keeps going until it finds a place where trade picks up again, and a new balance forms. The whole job of this method is to be at the edges of those balances.

Fair value, and the 70% convention
Statistically, one standard deviation around the mean holds about 68% of activity. Market Profile rounds it to 70%, which is why the value area is drawn around 70% of the volume, with the POC at its center. Prices outside it are the “unfair” ones where fewer people want to trade.
Balance is the common state
Markets spend most of their time rotating (people often quote 70 to 80%), so at the edge of a balance the first expectation is a rotation back inside, not an escape. A trend day is the exception that needs proof.
Acceptance
Price leaves an area and then trades there long enough, with volume, that it becomes the new neighborhood. Measure it in time and volume, not in one candle.
Rejection
Price touches an area and leaves fast, leaving a tail or a thin spot on the profile. The market has said “no”. These thin spots often get reused as levels later.
Eyeballing vs measuring
Looking at candles gives you a feel for balance and trend, but two traders will draw different boxes. Volume profile or TPO fixes the edges with numbers, so your levels are the same every day.

The 80% idea, as a drawing

The classic rule: if price opens outside yesterday’s value, comes back inside, and holds there (the usual test is two 30-minute periods), it often crosses the whole value area. Traders quote about 80%, but that is a rule of thumb from other markets and eras. Before you rely on it, test it on your own NQ data, because the real number may be quite different.

What can happen at the edge of value

OutcomeWhat you seeWhat it usually means
FadePrice touches the edge, then rotates backBalance holds, so use reversal or sweep setups
Break and acceptPrice goes out and builds volume thereNew value, so use break and retest
Fail and re-enterA poke outside, then back insideFailed auction, with the 80% idea in play
Chop at the edgeLots of small candles on the boundaryUndecided, so wait. This is the most common trap
For this method: only trade a digit level when it sits on one of these edges, and let the footprint tell you which of the four outcomes you are in.

Watch: specific AMT videos

▶ “Auction Market Theory” by JumpStart Trading (full video summary with timestamps, balance vs imbalance at 02:56)▶ FLW Weekly Class #1: Auction Market Theory (3rik)▶ Read: Auction theory for futures, pre-session checklist (NexusFi)

Volume profile and grading levels

A volume profile draws how much traded at each price, sideways. It shows where the market agreed on value and where it did not.

HVN and LVN
High volume nodes are prices where the market was comfortable, so price stalls or rotates there. Low volume nodes are prices it rejected, so price slices through them.
VAH, VAL and balance edges
In this method you mark the top and bottom of each balance by hand (VAH and VAL) on the weekly profile. Those are your “extremes”. The profile high and low are the outer extremes of the whole week.

Check the weekly profile first (5-minute, from last week’s high to low), then the daily profile if the weekly says nothing.

GradeWhere the digit level sitsUse
AAt a weekly balance edge or weekly extremeFull plan
BNot at a weekly edge, but at a daily profile edgeReduced size
CInside a balance, or in space with no volumeSkip
When price leaves the weekly range there is no weekly volume to read. Write a rule for it in advance (for example: use the daily profile only, half size) instead of improvising.
Figure B. The three profile shapes you will see most

Reading the profile step by step

  1. Mark last week’s high and low, then the weekly POC, VAH and VAL.
  2. Mark every LVN inside the range. These are fast zones, so do not plan a reversal in them.
  3. Mark yesterday’s POC, VAH and VAL on the daily profile.
  4. Note where the open sits: inside value, above, or below.
  5. List your digit levels, then circle only those within 15 points of a weekly or daily edge.

Naked POC: a prior day’s POC that price has not revisited yet. These often act as targets. Profile shape: D means balance, P short-covering up, b long liquidation down.

Volume profile, our way

You already know what POC, VAH and VAL are. This page is about using them for this method: deciding which digit levels deserve your attention.

Weekly first, daily second
The weekly profile is the map. The daily profile is the zoom. A digit level that matches both is your best trade. A level that matches neither is a coin flip, so skip it.
One session definition, always
Pick regular hours or the full session and never switch between them. Switching changes the POC and the edges, so your levels stop being comparable day to day.
Naked POCs
A previous POC that price has not come back to. These are natural targets. If your trade runs toward one, take profit before it, because prices tend to stall on the way in.
HVN and LVN rules
Fade a reaction at the outer edge of a high volume node. Never expect a reversal inside a low volume node, because price travels fast there. Use an LVN as the place where a break and retest setup is confirmed.
Profile shapes
Balanced (D), buyer-led (P), seller-led (b), and a double distribution with a thin gap between two humps. When the profile shifts value higher day after day, longs at pullbacks are favored. When it overlaps day after day, expect chop and take fewer trades.
Distance rule
A digit level counts only if it sits within about 15 points of a profile edge. Further than that, the profile is not backing it, and you are trading the digits alone.
Common mistakes: drawing the profile on too short a period, mixing session settings, treating every HVN as support, and ignoring that value moved. Redraw it on the same schedule every day.

The digit levels

The digits are NOT always 94. They come from yesterday’s high, so they change every day. 94 was only the example on Oct 30. Another day: high 29,731.50 gives digits 31, so the levels are 29,631 / 29,731 / 29,831. Use the calculator below with the real high every morning.
  1. Take yesterday’s high (sometimes the low too).
  2. Keep the last two digits: 30294 becomes 94.
  3. Mark that ending every 100 points near price: 30194, 30294, 30394.
  4. Watch only 9:30 to 11:00 ET.
  5. Grade each level on the volume profile, then pick a setup.
Level calculator

Honest check. NQ moves 300 to 500 points a day, so it crosses a level every 100 points constantly. Touches prove nothing. Test the same rules on random endings (17, 52, 68). If those perform just as well, the edge is not in the digits.

Three setups

A reaction is either a reversal off the level or a break followed by a retrace to it. Make each one its own rule, with numbers fixed before testing.

Reversal

Price touches the level and a candle closes back on the side it came from. Entry on that close. Stop beyond the level plus a buffer.

Break and retest

A candle closes beyond the level by X points, then price returns within N candles. Entry on the retest, stop back through the level. No retest means no trade, logged as “no setup”.

Sweep and reclaim

Price breaks the level, takes the stops, then closes back through. Entry after the reclaim close. Stop beyond the sweep extreme, which is known at entry.

One trade per level per day. Log every level, including the ones that did nothing.

Setup checklist, step by step

  1. Level graded A or B (weekly or daily balance edge).
  2. Price is at the level before 11:00 ET.
  3. Pattern is complete (reversal close, retest, or reclaim close). No half patterns.
  4. Footprint confirms: absorption, stacked imbalances, delta divergence.
  5. Stop is placed at a structure point and risk fits your daily loss limit.
  6. Target is the next level, POC or balance edge, at least 1.5R away.
Figure A. Sweep and reclaim (1-minute NQ, illustration; the 1R and 2R lines are to scale)

Risk = entry minus stop. Target = entry plus 1R and 2R. The sweep extreme is known before you enter, so the stop is a fact, not a guess.

Managing the trade
Move the stop to breakeven only after price closes past 1R, not before. Take half at 1R, leave half for the next level. If price returns to your entry and the footprint turns against you, exit. Never add to a loser.
Invalidation
A candle closing through the stop zone cancels the idea even before the stop is touched. Write the invalidation price in your gameplan.
Re-entry
One trade per level. A second attempt at a new level is allowed only if the first was a clean stop-out and you are under the daily loss limit.

Stops and position size

A flat 20-point stop makes little sense when NQ’s range changes every day. Use a stop that follows a rule: beyond the balance edge, beyond the sweep extreme, or a multiple of the recent average range. Then size the position from the stop, so every loss costs about the same.

Size calculator

R multiple
Result divided by the risk. Risking $300 and making $900 is +3R. Losing the stop is −1R. Logging in R lets you compare trades with different stop sizes.
A wide stop with a small size is fine. No defined stop is not. A move like the 1,000-plus point drop in late October is exactly why.

Footprint patterns: your 30%

Each pattern below answers one question: is the other side really there? You use them only at a level that scored well on the profile.

Setup the display first
Show bid x ask, delta per candle, and imbalance highlighting at about 300% with a minimum volume filter. Use the same settings every day, or you will not learn to recognize patterns.
Absorption
A very large number at one price and price refuses to travel. Confirm it by price failing to trade through the next candle.
Stacked imbalances
Three or more consecutive prices where one side dominates. Where they start often becomes a defended price when price returns.
Unfinished auction
At the extreme of a candle, one side has zero volume. The market usually comes back to finish the job, so avoid fading it immediately.
Delta divergence
New price extreme, but delta does not agree. A warning, never an entry on its own.
Exhaustion
Volume dries up as price pushes to a new extreme. The attackers have run out.
SetupFootprint you want
ReversalAbsorption at the level, then the next candle fails to extend
Break and retestStacked imbalances on the break, then a quiet pullback with no opposite stacks
Sweep and reclaimAggressive volume through the level that gets absorbed, then reclaim with delta flipping
Mistakes: seeing absorption everywhere (volume is high at every level on a busy day), trading without the level, changing settings after a loss, and judging a pattern from one candle. Review at least 20 examples per pattern before you trust it.

GEX and footprint

GEX (gamma exposure)

An estimate of how options dealers must hedge as price moves. Treat it as context, not a fact.

Gamma flip
The price where the estimate changes from positive to negative gamma.
Call wall and put wall
Strikes with heavy positioning above and below price, often acting as magnets or barriers.
Positive gamma
Dealers buy dips and sell rallies. Calmer, which favors reversal setups.
Negative gamma
Dealers add to moves. Larger swings, which favors break and retest.

Providers differ and 0DTE options complicate it. Use only the pre-market snapshot, credit the source (MentorQ), and check their terms before reposting their data.

Footprint

Shows bid and ask volume at every price inside each candle. It needs tick data.

Absorption
Heavy aggressive volume but price barely moves. Someone is soaking it up.
Stacked imbalances
Several prices in a row with one-sided volume (for example 300% or more). Shows who is in control.
Delta divergence
Price makes a new extreme but net buying or selling does not. A sign the move is tiring.
Add one filter at a time as a yes/no rule, and keep it only if it improves results on data you did not build it on. Two filters is plenty.

Footprint strategy confirmation

The footprint is a confirmation layer, never a signal by itself. The digit level and the volume-profile grade say where; the footprint says whether the other side is actually there. Wait for the level, then require these before entering:

  1. Absorption at the level: heavy aggressive volume into the digit level, price does not travel.
  2. Stacked imbalances in your direction right after (3 or more consecutive rows).
  3. Delta flips or diverges at the extreme: new price low, delta not making a new low.
  4. Failure to continue: next candle cannot trade through the absorbed price. This is your entry trigger.
  5. If any one is missing, no trade. Log it as “no confirmation”.
It takes time. Plan on a minimum of one month of daily screen time before footprint pattern recognition becomes reliable. Do not trade it live in month one. 
Week 1: read only, name the delta, stacked imbalance, absorption on 10 candles a day
Week 2: mark every digit level, screenshot each reaction, label what the footprint showed
Week 3: replay or sim, trade only A-grade levels with all 5 checks
Week 4: score yourself: confirmations that worked vs failed, then decide

The order flow toolkit

Order flow is not a strategy. It is the raw record of who did what. A chart shows where price went, and flow shows the fight that produced it.

Passive vs aggressive
Passive traders leave limit orders and wait. Aggressive traders pay the spread to get in now. Aggressive traders push price, and passive traders decide whether the push works.
Delta
Volume that hit the ask minus volume that hit the bid. 5,000 at the ask and 3,000 at the bid is +2,000. It tells you who was more urgent, not who won. Price up with negative delta means passive buyers absorbed the sellers.
Imbalance
One price where one side traded several times more than the other (the usual setting is 300% or higher). One imbalance is noise. Three or more in a row, stacked, show real pressure.
Absorption
Lots of aggressive volume, almost no movement. A wall of passive orders is soaking it up. It often marks a turn, but only after the wall is proven, which is why you wait for price to fail to continue.
Exhaustion
The opposite problem: the aggressors themselves run dry. Price makes a new extreme on weaker and weaker volume. Absorption is a strong defender. Exhaustion is a tired attacker.
Trapped traders
Late buyers at a high (or sellers at a low) who got in just before the reversal. Their stops fuel the move back, which is exactly the sweep and reclaim setup.
Cumulative delta and time and sales
Running delta over the session shows who is dominant overall. Time and sales shows the individual prints, useful for spotting unusually large ones.

AMD: accumulate, manipulate, distribute

Think of a range as a crowd of stops waiting above and below. Smart size tends to build in the range (accumulation), poke outside it to collect those stops (manipulation), then move the other way (distribution). Not every breakout is a trap, so the footprint decides: if the poke brings strong follow-through and no absorption, it is a real break. If aggressive volume gets absorbed and price snaps back, it was the trap. Use time too: the early range gives the levels, and the move out of it usually comes after. Sessions work the same way: Asia builds the range, London pokes it, New York often makes the run. Treat that as a tendency, never a schedule.

Iceberg orders

An iceberg is a big order shown in small slices. Each time a slice fills, a new one appears. You spot it in the footprint: heavy volume at one price, the displayed size keeps reloading, and price will not go through. It is absorption with a hidden engine behind it. Exchanges allow native iceberg orders, and some platforms simulate them. Detecting them reliably needs order-by-order data, so on a footprint just use the simple tell: lots of volume, no progress.

Options flow and gamma, in plain words

Dealers who sell options hedge by trading the underlying. How they hedge depends on what they hold, and that is what GEX tries to estimate. Several things change that hedge:

TermPlain meaningWhy you care on NQ
DeltaHow much the option moves per 1 point of the underlyingTotal delta is the hedge dealers carry
GammaHow fast delta changes as price movesShort gamma speeds moves up, long gamma slows them
VannaDelta change when volatility changesFalling volatility can pull in dealer hedges and lift the market
CharmDelta change as time passesHedges drift through the day, especially in the afternoon on expiry days
Vega, thetaOption price vs volatility and timeExplain why 0DTE decays so quickly
IVThe market’s priced expected moveWide IV means wider swings, so wider stops and smaller size
Open interestContracts still open at a strikeBig strikes become magnets or walls

The rarer ones (zomma, color, speed, ultima, vomma, rho, lambda) are second and third order tweaks of the same ideas. Know they exist. Do not trade from them. Sweeps, blocks and dark pool prints are large trades that show where money moved, but a big print never tells you its direction on its own. GARCH is a statistical forecast of volatility: useful for judging if the day is likely to be quiet or wild, useless for direction.

Your use: a pre-market glance at the gamma flip and walls (context for your levels), and nothing more.

DOM (depth of market): learn it, but do not use it on NQ

The DOM is a live ladder of resting buy and sell orders at each price. It shows intent, the orders people want to trade. The footprint shows what actually traded. That difference is the whole story.

Pulling
Resting orders vanish. The level is being abandoned, so a break through becomes more likely.
Stacking
More orders pile in at a price. Someone cares about that level, so it may act as support or resistance. Both are hints, never promises.
Why we do not use the DOM on NQ
  • Orders flicker. NQ’s book is mostly algorithms. Size appears and disappears in milliseconds, so much of what you see is never meant to trade.
  • Thin per level. A tick is 0.25 points and the book spreads across many prices, so a displayed size can look huge or tiny and mean nothing.
  • Your screen is slower than the market. Retail platforms throttle updates. By the time you react, the book changed.
  • Spoofing risk. Big orders placed only to be cancelled can mislead. The footprint cannot be faked: a trade either happened or it did not.
So: on NQ your confirmation comes from executed volume (the footprint), which is the 30% in this method.

ES is different. It has a deeper, steadier book with larger resting orders, so pulling and stacking and iceberg reading are more readable there. We do not trade ES here, but if you ever do, the DOM template is included in the Templates tab, and it is a fair place to practise.

Gameplan, recap and proof

Post this before 9:30 ET on a platform with visible timestamps, and never edit it afterward.

NQ GAMEPLAN [date, time ET]
Prev high / low: ____ / ____  Digit: __
Levels (near open): ____ ____ ____
Weekly profile: inside / edge / outside
Weekly & daily POC, VAH, VAL: ____
GEX (MentorQ, pre-market): flip ____ call wall ____ put wall ____
Grades: ____ = A/B/C
Scenario 1: if ____ then ____ ; wrong if ____
Scenario 2: if ____ then ____ ; wrong if ____
No-trade: ____
Not financial advice. Futures carry a high risk of loss.
RECAP [date]
Plan: played out / partly / failed
Levels touched ____ reacted ____ ran through ____
Trade: Y/N  result ___R  stop ___ pts
What I got wrong: ____

Pre-market routine (about 25 minutes)

Time (ET)Do
8:45News and calendar: any red-folder events before noon
8:50Mark prev high/low, digits, digit levels
9:00Weekly and daily profile, grade each level
9:10GEX snapshot: flip, call wall, put wall
9:15Write and post the gameplan with timestamp
9:30 to 11:00Trade only plan scenarios. Done by 11:00

Journal columns

Date, level, grade, setup, footprint checks passed (0 to 5), entry, stop, target, result in R, emotion before and after, followed the plan Y/N, screenshot link.

Test it before you trust it

  1. Define “reaction”, stops and targets in numbers before testing.
  2. Test 300 or more days, including commission and slippage.
  3. Run the placebo: same rules, random endings.
  4. Build on about 70% of days, then test the other 30% untouched.
  5. Report win rate, average win and loss, profit factor, drawdown, losing streaks, trade count.
  6. Keep the daily gameplan scoreboard (days with a plan, played out, failed, no trade, results in R by grade).
Keep an honest record. Timestamped plans, losing days included, and no income claims. Evaluation accounts are simulated, so only a payout actually received or a live account is real proof.

Example: Friday, Oct 30, 2026 (MNQ, 1-minute)

Yesterday’s high was 29,794.25, so the digits were 94. Levels marked: 28,694.25 and 28,894.75.

What happened
About 9:33 price pushed roughly 25 points below the level, then reclaimed it and rallied near 190 points to 28,862, stopping about 30 points under the upper level.
Setup
Sweep and reclaim. Entry after the close back above 28,694.25, stop under the sweep low, about 30 points of risk.
The stop lesson
A flat 20-point stop would have been hit. A stop under the sweep extreme survived.
Size
$300 risk and a 30-point stop is 5 MNQ. One full NQ contract would risk $600 on the same stop, so it does not fit. See the size calculator.
One day proves nothing, and winners are the ones people screenshot. Log this next to the days price ran through the level and never came back, and log 28,894.75 as “not reached”.

Trading psychology: the part that decides everything

Two minds, one trader

There is the planner and the executor. The planner works calmly when the market is closed. The executor is the part of you that acts when money is at risk, and it cares about escaping discomfort, not following your plan. A pilot does not trust mood in an emergency: they follow a checklist. Your plan is that checklist, which is why we wrote the 100-point score and the one-trade rule before the session.

Judge the process, not the money

A win that broke your rules is a bad trade, and a loss that followed them is a good one. After each session, score yourself yes or no: right level, footprint confirmed, stop respected, size respected, one trade only. Five yes answers means a good day, whatever the P&L says.

Revenge trading
Taking a trade right after a loss just to get the money back. It skips your process, so it usually loses more. Our method makes it a rule: one trade a day, and when it is done, you are done.
FOMO
Price hit your level, went without you, and now you want in. Chasing it gives you a worse entry and a wider stop. Mark it “missed”, write what you would change, and wait. Setups come every week.
Overtrading
Taking trades that do not meet your score. Every extra trade adds cost and fatigue and pulls you toward random. For us, doing nothing on a no-setup day is a good trade.
Tilt
Your emotions are so high that you are gambling. Body signs: fast heartbeat, tight jaw or shoulders, shallow breathing. Behavior signs: rapid clicking, moving the stop, checking the P&L constantly. Two or more signs, and you stop now.
Discipline is trained
Pick one rule and follow it for 20 straight sessions before adding a second. Stack rules slowly.
Realistic expectations
Even good systems lose a large share of their trades, and drawdowns can last weeks. Use process targets (follow the plan, journal daily, review weekly) instead of daily money targets, which push you to force trades.

Weekly review: five questions

  1. How many trades broke my rules, and when?
  2. What was my emotional state before each loss?
  3. Which setups did I see and not take?
  4. What is my biggest repeated leak?
  5. What is the one rule I follow next week?

Watch

▶ Trading psychology▶ Mental game▶ Trading discipline

The last lesson: you are the strategy

Football. A team goes 1-0 up and the plan is simple: hold shape, keep the ball. Then a player gets angry about a foul, ignores the plan, chases a tackle, gets a red card. The tactics were fine. The ego lost the match.

Boxing. The coach says: jab, move, protect the chin. Then the fighter gets hit once, gets angry, and starts swinging wildly. He stops following the plan and walks into the knockout. A loss is not what puts you on the canvas. Ignoring the plan after a loss does.

Trading. Same story. Stop hit, you want it back, you double size, take a second trade, move the stop. That is the red card and the wild swing.
  • One trade a day means the plan ends when the trade ends. Closing the platform is part of the strategy.
  • Rules written before the session beat decisions made in it.
  • A loss that followed the plan is a good trade. A win that broke the plan is a bad one, and you should log it as such.
  • Blame is a trap. If you blame the market, the firm or the author, you stop looking at the only thing you can change.
A personal note. I did not build this to impress you. I built it because I want you to do well, and ideally better than me. Follow the plan when it is boring, accept the losses without drama, and you will have a real shot. Respect the process, and the process will respect you.

The one-trade-a-day prop-firm method

The idea: stop grinding for weeks. Pass the evaluation fast, then hunt one big winning day per day, one trade maximum, and be done. It is a high-variance plan, so it needs written limits more than any other part of this playbook.

RuleSetting
Trades per day1 maximum. Win or lose, you are done
Risk / targetRisk at most half the daily loss limit, target 2R (1:2)
Passing the evaluationA few A-grade days, sized to the firm’s rules, no oversizing
After a big winnerSecure it: close the platform, no second trade
Daily loss limit (DLL)Set from your firm’s rules (example: $300)
Quality filterA-grade digit level, weekly profile edge, footprint confirmation (all 5 checks)
Why risk must stay under the daily loss limit.
1. Risking $2,000 per trade with a $300 DLL means one loss breaches the account. Risk per trade can never exceed the DLL, or your firm’s trailing drawdown.
2. “No stop loss” means the loss is whatever the market gives you. On NQ, 100 points is $2,000 per contract, and fast days move far more. The DLL is enforced after the damage, so it is not a stop.
3. 1:2 needs a win rate above 33.3% just to break even, before commissions. One trade a day also means few samples, so results swing hard.
4. Many firms have consistency rules and cap how much one day can be of total profit. Read yours before building the plan on one big day.
The rule: pick the stop first (beyond the sweep extreme or balance edge), then size so the loss at that stop is at most 50% of the DLL. With a $300 DLL that is $150 of risk and a $300 target. End the day at +1R or −0.5R and stop either way.
Figure C. Risk per trade versus the daily loss limit (example: $300 DLL)

A full day, step by step

  1. Pre-market: grade levels and post the plan. If nothing is A-grade, the day is a no-trade day.
  2. 9:30 to 10:30: wait for price to reach an A level. Do not chase.
  3. Pattern completes and the footprint confirms: enter with the stop in a structure point.
  4. Risk is set first: stop distance times contracts must be at most half the DLL.
  5. Target the next level. Take half at 1R, hold half.
  6. Winner or loser, you are done after this one trade. Close the platform.
  7. Recap with screenshots before bed.
Passing the evaluation fast
Size to the firm’s rules, not to your hopes. A fast pass comes from a few A-grade days, not from oversizing. Check the profit target, trailing drawdown, consistency rule, and minimum trading days for your firm.
After you are funded
Payouts depend on the firm’s rules and your actual results. Nothing here promises a number of winning days or a payout.

Track this as its own log: trades, R result, days breached or near-breached, and payouts actually received. Keep the losing days in it too.
